h1: Cacao nibs in stout and porter: dose, timing and sanitising
title: Cacao Nibs in Stout and Porter | Craft Beer School
desc: How to use cacao nibs in stout and porter: dose per litre, when to add them, how to sanitise nibs and why cocoa powder is a poor substitute.
teaser: Cacao nibs give a stout real chocolate aroma without sugar. Here is how much to use, when and how to keep them clean.
standfirst: Roasted malts already give stout a chocolate edge. Cacao nibs add real cocoa aroma on top, dry rather than sweet, like good dark chocolate. Used well, they turn a decent stout into something memorable. Here is the method, including the sanitising step most recipes skip.
sections:
Cacao nibs are pieces of fermented, dried and usually roasted cacao beans, the raw material of chocolate. They contain cocoa solids and cocoa butter but no sugar or milk. In beer they give cocoa aroma and a light, dry bitterness. They do not make the beer sweet.

India grows cacao, mainly in Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Several small Indian chocolate makers sell nibs from Indian beans. Different origins taste different: some fruity, some earthy, some with a roasted coffee note. Taste a few before you brew. Store them in an airtight jar in the fridge, because cocoa butter turns stale and rancid in a warm Indian kitchen. That stale note carries straight into the beer.

Cocoa powder is easy to find, but it is a poor beer ingredient. It does not dissolve well and settles as sludge in the fermenter and bottles. Its flavour is also flatter than nibs. Chocolate bars are worse: the sugar ferments away while the cocoa butter and milk solids hurt foam and clarity.

Nibs extract cleanly over a few days and come out with the dry hops or the racking, leaving clear beer behind.

The common starting dose is about 5 to 10 g of nibs per litre, so 100 to 200 g in a 20 litre batch. For a big imperial stout with lots of roast and alcohol, go towards the top of that range or beyond. For a lighter porter, the lower end.

Timing matters:

  • In the boil: extracts some bitterness and colour, but most of the aroma boils away. Not recommended as the only addition.
  • After primary fermentation: the best option for aroma. Add nibs for 3 to 7 days, tasting every couple of days, then remove.
  • Tincture at packaging: soak nibs in a neutral spirit for a week, then add the strained liquid to taste. This gives precise control and keeps everything sanitary.

Taste regularly during contact. After a week or so, nibs can start to give a harsh, tannic bitterness.

Nibs are dry and roasted, so the risk of contamination is low, but not zero. Adding them to beer after fermentation means no boil to clean them up. Three common methods:

  1. Spirit soak. Cover the nibs in a neutral spirit such as vodka for a day or two. Add nibs and spirit to the fermenter. The small amount of spirit is negligible in 20 litres.
  2. Oven toast. Spread nibs on a tray and toast at about 120 to 150 °C for 10 minutes. This also deepens the roast character. Watch them, as they burn quickly.
  3. Brief steam. Hold nibs over boiling water in a sieve for a few minutes. Less common, but it works.

Whichever you choose, put the nibs in a sanitised mesh bag so they are easy to remove. Our guide to brewing a stout at home covers the base beer.
Does cocoa butter hurt head retention?

Nibs contain a lot of fat, roughly half their weight. Fat is bad for foam. At normal doses, very little of it ends up in the beer, because cocoa butter does not dissolve well in cold beer and stays in the nibs. Brewers using sensible amounts rarely see a noticeable effect on head.

If you see an oily film or poor foam, try a tincture next time. The spirit pulls out aroma while leaving most of the fat behind.

Cacao nibs work well with:

  • Coffee: the classic mocha stout. Our guide to adding coffee to beer covers cold-brew additions.
  • Vanilla: half a split pod per 20 litres rounds out cocoa nicely.
  • Chilli: a Mexican-style chocolate stout with a little heat. Add chilli last and in tiny amounts.
  • Orange peel: chocolate orange, especially in a porter.

Add one flavour at a time and taste before committing. In a big imperial stout the base beer can carry more, but adjuncts stack up quickly.

Adjunct work is mostly about extraction and timing: how long an ingredient sits, at what temperature and how clean it is. Get those right and the base beer you designed stays in charge.
faqs: How many cacao nibs per litre of beer?
Start at about 5 to 10 g per litre, so 100 to 200 g for 20 litres. Taste during contact and remove when it is right.
When should I add cacao nibs?
After primary fermentation for 3 to 7 days gives the best aroma. A spirit tincture at packaging gives the most control.
Do I need to sanitise cacao nibs?
It is good practice. Soak them in a neutral spirit, toast them briefly in the oven or steam them before adding.
Will cacao nibs make my stout sweet?
No. Nibs contain no sugar. They add cocoa aroma and a dry bitterness.
